column9: Used to indicate that one is speaking in an open, honest, and direct manner, often introducing a critical or blunt statement.
column10: Frankly, I don't care what they think about my decision.
column11: He frankly admitted that he had made a huge mistake during the negotiations.
column12: Quite frankly, the service at that restaurant was absolutely terrible.

column9: Used to convey that what is asserted is very likely though not known for certain; it is reasonable to assume.
column10: Presumably, he's going to be late as he hasn't arrived yet and there is traffic.
column11: The meeting has been cancelled, presumably because of the low attendance numbers.
column12: Presumably, you've already read the report, so I won't go through it in detail.

column9: Used when a person has something more to say, or is about to add a remark not connected with the current subject; by the way.
column10: Incidentally, did you hear about the election results while you were away?
column11: I saw John yesterday at the supermarket. Incidentally, he still owes me money.
column12: The report was well written, incidentally, even though the conclusion was wrong.

column9: Used to express pleasure or relief that something has happened (Sentence Adverb meaning 'fortunately'); distinct from 'in a happy way'.
column10: Happily, he didn't die in the accident and made a full recovery.
column11: Happily, the weather stayed fine for the wedding despite the forecast.
column12: She happily accepted the invitation to the party. (Manner adverb contrast).

column9: Used to show that something is obvious or certain; without doubt.
column10: Clearly, you don't know what you're doing if you pressed that button.
column11: It is clearly a mistake to invest all your money in one stock.
column12: Clearly, we need to rethink our strategy before the next quarter.

column9: Used to state that one has heard that something is true, although one is not completely certain (hearsay).
column10: Apparently, it's going to rain later, so bring an umbrella.
column11: She has resigned, apparently, though there has been no official announcement.
column12: Apparently, they are getting divorced after twenty years of marriage.

column9: It is fortunate that; luckily.
column10: Fortunately, I had my umbrella with me when the storm started.
column11: Fortunately, no one was hurt in the fire at the warehouse.
column12: We arrived late, but fortunately the movie hadn't started yet.

column9: Giving someone support or confidence; supportive; positive.
column10: We haven't seen a massive improvement yet, but a 2% rise is quite encouraging.
column11: The doctor gave us an encouraging report on his health progress.
column12: It is encouraging to see so many young people voting in the election.

column9: Large and heavy or solid; exceptionally large.
column10: We haven't seen a massive improvement in sales yet, but it's early days.
column11: They have a massive house in the country with ten bedrooms.
column12: The project was a massive success, earning millions for the company.

column9: To succeed in entering a market or profession; to enter a building illegally.
column10: It's hard to break into the Korean market because of the strong local competition.
column11: She is trying to break into the music industry, but it is very competitive.
column12: The company struggled to break into the US market for years.

column9: To pass responsibility or control to someone else.
column10: I'll make three points, and then I'll hand you over to David for the financial details.
column11: He handed over the leadership to his deputy after ten years in charge.
column12: Can you hand over that file, please? I need to check something.

column9: To arrive at a destination (often used for trains, flights, or people arriving home/work).
column10: I'm getting in at 10:00 AM, not PM, so I'll meet you for lunch.
column11: What time does your train get in to London Euston?
column12: I got in late last night because of the flight delay.

column9: Luggage that is stored in the cargo hold of an aircraft rather than carried into the cabin.
column10: The first checked bag is free on this airline, but you pay for the second.
column11: Do you have any checked bags or just carry-on luggage?
column12: My checked bag was lost by the airline and arrived three days later.

column9: The quality of being open to more than one interpretation; inexactness.
column10: Pausing prevents ambiguity in sentences like 'She dressed and fed the baby'.
column11: There is some ambiguity in the contract wording regarding the termination clause.
column12: We need to remove any ambiguity from the instructions so everyone understands.

column9: The conclusion that can be drawn from something although it is not explicitly stated.
column10: The implication of his tone was that he didn't believe a word I said.
column11: What are the implications of this decision for the future of the company?
column12: Contrastive stress can change the implication of a sentence entirely.

column9: To deny the truth of (a statement) by asserting the opposite.
column10: He contradicted my statement immediately in front of the boss.
column11: The evidence contradicts his story about where he was that night.
column12: You can use sentence stress to contradict someone: 'I didn't say WE should kill him'.

column9: To make (a statement or situation) less confused and more comprehensible.
column10: Could you clarify what you mean by 'soon'? Do you mean today or next week?
column11: I need to clarify a few points before we proceed with the project.
column12: Stress is used to clarify which part of the sentence is most important.

column9: The rise and fall of the voice in speaking.
column10: Intonation can change a statement into a question without changing the word order.
column11: Her flat intonation made her sound bored and uninterested.
column12: Paying attention to intonation helps you understand the speaker's true attitude.

column9: Stress placed on a word to highlight a contrast or difference from another word or idea.
column10: In the sentence 'I didn't say we should kill him', placing stress on 'I' is an example of contrastive stress.
column11: Use contrastive stress to correct a misunderstanding or emphasize a specific point.
column12: Contrastive stress implies that someone else might have said it, if you stress 'I'.

column9: A clause that gives essential information to define or identify the person or thing being talked about (no commas/pauses).
column10: In 'My brother who lives in Grimsby', the clause 'who lives in Grimsby' is a defining relative clause identifying which brother.
column11: Defining relative clauses are not separated by commas in writing or pauses in speech.
column12: It tells us *which* brother we are talking about, implying there is more than one.

column9: A clause that gives extra, non-essential information about a person or thing (uses commas/pauses).
column10: In 'My brother, who lives in Grimsby...', the clause is non-defining and adds extra detail.
column11: Non-defining relative clauses are separated by commas in writing and pauses in speech.
column12: This implies I only have one brother, and incidentally, he lives in Grimsby.

column9: A short question at the end of a statement, used to seek confirmation or agreement (e.g., isn't it?, don't you?).
column10: 'You're coming, aren't you?' is a tag question that checks for information or agreement.
column11: Intonation on tag questions changes the meaning from a real question to just seeking agreement.
column12: Falling intonation on a tag question asks for agreement, not an answer.

column9: The highest level of managers in an organization.
column10: All three points concern senior management and their strategic decisions.
column11: She was promoted to senior management after ten years of service.
column12: Major decisions are always made by senior management, not the team leaders.

column2: I didn't say we should kill him.
column9: A sentence used to demonstrate how stress changes meaning.
column10: 'I' didn't say we should kill him. (Someone else said it).
column11: I didn't 'say' we should kill him. (I might have thought it, or implied it).
column12: I didn't say we should 'kill' him. (We should do something else to him, like fire him).

column9: Sentence adverb used to introduce a blunt opinion.
column10: Frankly, I don't care what happens to the project now.
column11: I don't care, frankly. (Adverb at the end acts as an afterthought).
column12: I spoke to him frankly about his bad behaviour. (Manner adverb - different meaning).

column2: My brother who lives in Grimsby is a politician.
column9: Defining relative clause (no pauses) identifying one specific brother.
column10: Implies the speaker has more than one brother, and this specific one is the politician.
column11: My brother who lives in London is a doctor, but my brother who lives in Grimsby is a politician.
column12: (No commas in writing, no pauses in speech).

column2: My brother, who lives in Grimsby, is a politician.
column9: Non-defining relative clause (with pauses) giving extra information.
column10: Implies the speaker has only one brother.
column11: The extra information is that he lives in Grimsby, but the main point is he is a politician.
column12: (Commas in writing, pauses in speech).

column2: She dressed and fed the baby.
column9: Without a pause: She put clothes on the baby and fed the baby.
column10: Standard interpretation: She performed both actions on the baby.
column11: There is no ambiguity here if spoken fluently without a break.

column2: She dressed, and fed the baby.
column9: With a pause after 'dressed': She put clothes on herself, and then fed the baby.
column10: The comma/pause changes the object of the verb 'dressed' to be reflexive (herself).
column11: Illustrates the importance of pausing for clarity in storytelling.

column2: The Panda eats, shoots and leaves.
column9: With commas/pauses: The Panda eats a meal, fires a gun, and departs.
column10: Without commas: The Panda eats bamboo shoots and leaves (plants).
column11: A famous example of how punctuation/pausing changes meaning from a description of diet to a crime scene.

column2: We need apples, pears, bananas and cheese.
column9: Demonstrates list intonation: Rising, Rising, Rising, Falling.
column10: Apples (up), pears (up), bananas (up), and cheese (down).
column11: Falling intonation on the last item signals the list is finished.

column2: Do you think it's better to buy or rent this car?
column9: Open question: Buy (up) or rent (down)? (Choice question).
column10: Implies a choice between two specific options and you must pick one.
column11: Closed question: Buy or rent (up)? (Implies 'or do something else?').

column2: Does she know that, or is she just guessing?
column9: Alternative question requiring a specific choice between two options.
column10: Does she know that (up), or is she just guessing (down)?
column11: Intonation signals that one of these must be true and you should select one.

column2: I'm getting in at 10:00 AM, not PM.
column9: Stressing 'AM' and 'PM' to clarify a misunderstanding about time.
column10: I said ten AM, not PM.
column11: Corrective stress focuses on the difference between morning and evening.

column2: The first checked bag is free on this airline.
column9: Stressing 'first' implies the second one is not free.
column10: Stressing 'checked' implies carry-on bags might have different rules.
column11: Stressing 'free' highlights the benefit compared to paying.

column2: It's hard to break into the Korean market.
column9: Stressing 'hard' emphasizes the difficulty level.
column10: Stressing 'Korean' contrasts it with other markets (e.g., 'The Japanese market is easy, but the Korean one...').
column11: 'Break into' means to enter a market successfully.

column2: I'll hand you over to David.
column9: To pass control of the conversation/meeting to David.
column10: Common in presentations: 'I'll hand you over to David for the next part.'
column11: I'll hand over to my colleague now to explain the technical details.

column2: We haven't seen a massive improvement yet.
column9: Stressing 'massive' implies there has been *some* improvement, but not a big one.
column10: Stressing 'yet' implies we expect to see one soon.
column11: Stressing 'seen' might imply there is an improvement but it's not visible.

column9: The quality of a sound governed by the rate of vibrations producing it; the degree of highness or lowness of a tone.
column10: Intonation involves changing the pitch of your voice to signal meaning.
column11: A high pitch usually indicates a question or uncertainty in English.
column12: He spoke in a low pitch which made him sound serious.

column9: Emphasis given to a particular syllable or word in speech.
column10: Changing the stress can completely change the meaning of the sentence.
column11: English is a stress-timed language, which dictates its rhythm.
column12: Put the stress on the second syllable for the verb 'record'.

column9: To interrupt action or speech briefly.
column10: You need to pause after the non-defining relative clause to indicate the comma.
column11: He paused for effect before delivering the punchline.
column12: She paused to catch her breath after running up the stairs.

column9: A punctuation mark (,) indicating a pause between parts of a sentence.
column10: A comma in writing corresponds to a short pause in speech.
column11: Non-defining relative clauses are always marked by commas.
column12: The Oxford comma is optional but can clarify lists.

column9: A word whose purpose is more to signal grammatical relationship than the lexical meaning (e.g., do, the, of).
column10: Function words are usually unstressed in English connected speech.
column11: Prepositions, pronouns, and articles are typical function words.
column12: Contrast function words with content words which carry the meaning.

column9: A word that conveys information in a text or speech act (e.g., nouns, verbs, adjectives).
column10: Content words typically receive stress in a sentence.
column11: Nouns, main verbs, adjectives, and adverbs are content words.
column12: Focus on the content words to understand the core message of the sentence.

column9: A verb used in forming the tenses, moods, and voices of other verbs (e.g., be, do, have).
column10: Auxiliary verbs often have weak forms in connected speech unless they are stressed for emphasis.
column11: 'Do' is an auxiliary verb in 'Do you like it?'.
column12: Modals are also auxiliary verbs and often contracted.

column9: Estimating or supposing something without sufficient information to be sure of being correct.
column10: Is she just guessing or does she know for a fact?
column11: I'm just guessing, but I think the answer is option B.
column12: Stop guessing and find the actual answer in the book.

column9: A particular place or position.
column10: The location is perfect, but the price is too high.
column11: We need to find a suitable location for the meeting.
column12: Can you send me your location on the map?

column9: To pay someone for the use of something.
column10: Do you think it's better to buy or rent this car?
column11: We decided to rent a flat in the city instead of buying.
column12: He rents his house out to tourists in the summer.

column9: To relate to; be about.
column10: These three points concern senior management and their responsibilities.
column11: This issue doesn't concern you, so please stay out of it.
column12: The book concerns the history of the war in Europe.

column9: To move forward or develop towards a goal.
column10: I think we're making progress with the negotiations.
column11: We are making slow progress on the project due to lack of funds.
column12: She has made great progress in her English studies this year.

column9: At this point in a process or activity.
column10: It's very difficult to say what will happen at this stage.
column11: We can't confirm anything at this stage of the investigation.
column12: At this stage of the competition, anything can happen.

column2: He washed and brushed his hair.
column9: Without pause: He washed his hair and brushed his hair. (Reflexive implied for both).
column10: With pause after 'washed': He washed himself (body), and then brushed his hair.
column11: Standard interpretation without pause is applying 'hair' to both verbs.

column9: Stressing 'Denmark' contrasts it with other countries (e.g., 'They sell in Sweden, but not Denmark').
column10: Our products sell in Sweden, but they don't sell in DENMARK.
column11: Implies a specific problem with that market compared to others.

column9: Stressing 'enough' modifies the meaning of 'sell' to mean 'sell in sufficient quantities'.
column10: They sell, but not in sufficient quantities to make a profit.
column11: Correction of the idea that they don't sell at all - they do, just not enough.

column9: Falling intonation on 'aren't you': Expects agreement.
column10: 'I know you are coming, just confirm it for me.'
column11: Sounds more like a statement of fact than a real question.

column9: Rising intonation on 'aren't you': A genuine question needing an answer.
column10: 'I am not sure if you are coming, please tell me yes or no.'
column11: Sounds uncertain and requires clarification.

column2: I didn't say we should kill *him*.
column9: Stressing 'him' implies we should kill someone else.
column10: Demonstrates how stress isolates the object of the sentence.
column11: Changes the victim in the sentence from 'him' to another person.

column2: I didn't say we *should* kill him.
column9: Stressing 'should' implies it's a possibility, but not a necessity or obligation.
column10: Or implies 'I said we *could* kill him', not that we must.
column11: Focuses on the modal verb nuance between suggestion and obligation.

column2: I didn't *say* we should kill him.
column9: Stressing 'say' implies I might have written it, thought it, or implied it, but not spoken it.
column10: Denies the specific act of speaking the words.
column11: Often used to be pedantic or defensive about exactly what was spoken.

column2: I *didn't* say we should kill him.
column9: Stressing 'didn't' strongly denies the whole statement.
column10: Used when someone accuses you of saying it and you want to deny it properly.
column11: A strong denial of the entire accusation.

column2: I didn't say *we* should kill him.
column9: Stressing 'we' implies someone else should do it.
column10: 'They should do it, not us.'
column11: Shifts responsibility from the speaker's group to another group.

column9: 'Presumably' indicates a logical guess based on evidence.
column10: Intonation usually falls after 'Presumably' to separate it.
column11: He isn't here, so I presume he missed the bus (likely explanation).

column9: 'Incidentally' changes the topic or adds a side note.
column10: Used to introduce a side comment that isn't the main point.
column11: By the way, I like your coat (unrelated to previous topic).

column9: 'Happily' means 'It is a happy fact that...' (Sentence Adverb).
column10: Fortunately, the rain stopped before the picnic.
column11: Different from 'He played happily' which describes the manner of playing.

column9: 'Apparently' means 'I have heard/read that...' (Hearsay).
column10: It seems she is pregnant, according to rumors.
column11: Distances the speaker from the fact (it's not firsthand knowledge).

column9: Stressing 'location' contrasts it with other aspects (like price).
column10: The *location* is perfect, but the *price* is wrong.
column11: Positive aspect highlighted to contrast with a negative one later.

column2: I'm not sure about the price.
column9: Stressing 'price' highlights the negative aspect.
column10: The location is good, but the *price* is the problem.
column11: Expressing hesitation about a specific factor.

column2: It's hard to break into the Japanese market.
column9: Stressing 'Japanese' contrasts with 'Korean' or other markets.
column10: It's even *harder* to break into the *Japanese* one compared to the Chinese one.
column11: Comparative difficulty between two specific markets.

column2: There are three points I'd like to make.
column9: Standard phrase for introducing a list in a presentation.
column10: Stressing 'three' signals the structure of the talk to the audience.
column11: Clear signposting helps the listener follow the argument.

column2: I don't think that's a good idea.
column9: Stressing 'I' implies 'Others might agree, but *I* don't'.
column10: Stressing 'that's' implies 'Other ideas are good, but *that* specific one isn't'.
column11: Stressing 'good' implies 'It's an *okay* idea, but not *good*'.

column9: Stressing 'guessing' focuses on the reliability of the information.
column10: Is she sure, or just *guessing*? (Doubt).
column11: Highlights uncertainty about the person's knowledge.

column9: A subtle difference in or shade of meaning, expression, or sound.
column10: Intonation adds nuance to your speech that text cannot convey.
column11: We need to appreciate the nuances of the language to be fluent.
column12: He didn't catch the nuance of her remark and was offended.

column9: Excessively concerned with minor details or rules; over-scrupulous.
column10: Correcting someone's grammar in a casual conversation can seem pedantic.
column11: He is very pedantic about punctuation usage.
column12: A pedantic interpretation of the rules led to the rejection.

column9: Very anxious to challenge or avoid criticism.
column10: He became defensive when I asked about the mistake in the report.
column11: Using stress on 'say' ('I didn't *say*...') can sound defensive.
column12: Don't be so defensive, I'm just asking a question.

column9: (Of a person or remark) uncompromisingly forthright.
column10: 'Frankly' introduces a blunt statement that might offend.
column11: He was very blunt about my performance review.
column12: To be blunt, your work is not good enough.

column9: Information received from other people which cannot be substantiated; rumour.
column10: 'Apparently' indicates the statement is based on hearsay.
column11: The evidence was dismissed as hearsay by the judge.
column12: I don't believe it; it's just hearsay until I see proof.

column9: Using phrases to guide the listener through a presentation (e.g., 'There are three points...').
column10: Good signposting makes a presentation easier to follow for the audience.
column11: Use signposting to structure your argument clearly.
column12: 'First of all', 'Secondly' are examples of signposting language.

column9: Luggage that is taken into the cabin of an aircraft.
column10: I only have carry-on luggage for this short trip.
column11: Is this bag small enough for carry-on limits?
column12: Carry-on liquids must be under 100ml.

column9: A person appointed to undertake the duties of a superior in the superior's absence.
column10: He handed over control to his deputy while he was away.
column11: She is the deputy head teacher of the school.
column12: The deputy director took charge of the department.
